notes.title: Chapter map: Thinking

headings.text: ⏱️ Working with preemptive generation: everything that starts early
🌳 Decide: what may run after the turn commits?

notes.html:
How the agent decides what to say without making the person wait for it. One principle runs through every note: anything that can start while the person is still talking should, and whatever is left on the critical path must have a deadline and a fallback.

Where this sits

capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe

Working with preemptive generation: everything that starts early

All of these start on the same signal, a final transcript phrase, while the endpoint wait is still running (endpointing). They must agree on one thing: the turn number.

Starts on the final phrase Note If the person keeps talking Ready at commit?
Draft reply (preemptive generation) 027 discarded, the turn runs again usually: the model is hidden in the wait
Guard label 033 re-run on the fuller text usually; else held ≤ 0.9 s, then released
Background analysis (Assessor, Prober) 031 restarted, debounced 300 ms sometimes; else the picker's rule
Speculative moves (design) 030 refreshed by design; else the planned question

Rules that keep them consistent: every write is keyed by turn and overwrites · the picker reads only earlier turns · progress counts only moves the person heard · background results live outside the graph state so they can't race the checkpoint · the guard labels, the picker decides.

Reading order

# Note Tier Stage You'll understand
1 The model on the hot path CORE think why TTFT is the network from India, and the levers that shrink it
2 Speculative pre-generation CORE think how the design removes the model call: select, don't generate
3 Latency-tiered agents SUPPORTING think T0 in the turn, T1 during speech, T2 after the call
4 Guardrails beside the reply SUPPORTING think draft and hold: safety without a serial step
5 Writing for the ear SUPPORTING think the prompt rules for spoken output; exact text outside the model
6 Persona and personality SUPPORTING think one character in words, voice and timing; neutral where answers are judged
7 Tools and slow work SUPPORTING think async tools, fillers, never leaving silence
8 External tools and MCP SUPPORTING think few tools, timeouts, read-back before writes, MCP toolsets in a spoken turn

Owners

Concept Home
TTFT on the critical path, hot-path model choice, token caps model on the hot path
Pre-drafted moves, selection at commit, the fallback ladder, hit rate speculative pre-generation
T0 / T1 / T2, insights keyed by turn, questioner ≠ scorer latency-tiered agents
Spoken-output rules, verbatim tails, fillers vs latency writing for the ear
Identity, stance, tone per moment, fixed lines in the same voice, emotion control persona and personality
Draft-and-hold guard, fail open, fixed lines for guarded moves guardrails beside the reply
Async tools, filler audio, results out of turn tools and slow work
External tools and MCP servers in a voice turn: count, timeouts, read-back, MCPToolset external tools and MCP
MCP itself: protocol, transports, auth, security Protocols & interoperability (agentic)
Preemptive generation itself and its idempotency rules preemptive generation
035 → pointer: agent-graph design for voice (graph shape, LangGraph vs LiveKit handoffs) voice agents · conversational and interview agents · livekit_decision The LangGraph seam
Latency of agentic systems in general latency in agentic systems

Decide: what may run after the turn commits?

Ask in order If yes → Because
1. Can it be prepared while the person speaks? background tier, keyed by turn speech time is free
2. Is it a check on the reply, not the reply? run beside the draft, hold briefly, fail open a serial check taxes every turn
3. Must the words be exact? fixed text, no model a model may change them
4. Otherwise one streamed call: small model, token cap, deadline, fallback line it's the critical path

🔊 Our system in one table

Stage What we run Status Measured
think rules pick the move, Cerebras gpt-oss-120b phrases it, planned question appended verbatim TTFT p50 442 ms, p95 1 714 ms
think preemptive generation on; guard, T1 and draft start on the final phrase hit rate not measured
think Gatekeeper qwen-3.8-27b, hold 0.9 s, fail open 340 ms – 2.6 s; rules 2/37 vs model 36–37/37
think T1 Assessor + Prober (gpt-4.1-mini) during speech Prober probes 62% of complete answers
think speculative pre-generation, selection in ~10 ms –

Landscape (as of Oct 2026)

Option Where Note
Preemptive generation LiveKit Agents, on by default preemptive_tts off by default
Async tools, filler audio LiveKit Agents ctx.update, ctx.with_filler
Per-modality instructions LiveKit Agents (beta) Instructions(audio=…, text=…)
Fast hot-path inference e.g. Cerebras, Groq (both used or evaluated here) measure TTFT from your region

Game Day

Q32 LLM in the hot path · Q39 multi-agent in the loop · Q40 Chair is rules · Q41 Prober not ready · Q42 intent detection

notes.title: The Model on the Hot Path — Time to First Token in a Spoken Turn
notes.html:
References

~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/as_built.md §3 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/utkarsh_architecture.md §2 · ~/Projects/convo_agentic/meghdootam/brain/llms.py · LiveKit — Data hooks

TL;DR

Any model call that starts after the turn is committed adds its time to first token straight onto the silence the person hears. Only the first token matters (the voice can start on the first sentence), and from a far region that time is mostly network, not the model.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per turn

Flow: turn committedrequestprovider queuefirst tokenfirst sentenceTTS

Recall

Prompt Answer
Which latency of the model counts? time to first token (TTFT) of a streamed reply, not the full reply
What makes TTFT from India slow? the network and the provider's queue, not inference
Why does p95 run far above p50? the provider's queue under load
Three ways to take the model off the hot path pre-generate during speech, select instead of generate, start on the final phrase (preemptive)
What to say when the model is late? a fixed line or the planned question, never silence
Draw the turn with the model on vs off the hot path on: endpoint → TTFT → TTS; off: endpoint → select (~10 ms) → TTS

The idea

Without a plan for it: the reply model runs after commit, its median and its tail both land in the gap, and a vendor's bad minute becomes the product's bad minute.

It does: treats the model call as a budget line with a deadline, a smaller and closer model for the hot path, and a design goal of removing it altogether.

It costs: the best fix (pre-generation) needs a different architecture; the cheap fixes (preemptive generation, a fast provider) shrink the line but leave it there.

How it works

Lever Saves Cost
Stream, speak the first sentence the rest of the reply's generation time sentence chunking (07 Speaking)
Short outputs (one or two sentences, a token cap) generation after the first token reasoning models spend hidden tokens first; the cap must leave room
Preemptive generation TTFT on turns that commit with the same words wasted calls
Fast provider, in region the network and the queue a second vendor to run
Pre-generate during speech and select at commit the whole line the design in speculative pre-generation

Knobs

Knob Typical Raise it → Lower it →
Max output tokens small for speech room for reasoning and the reply truncated or empty replies on reasoning models
Reasoning effort lowest that keeps quality better replies, later first word faster first word
Retries on the hot path 0–1 survives a blip, doubles the wait fails fast to the fallback
Deadline before the fallback ~1 s fewer fallbacks more scripted lines

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Speaker model Cerebras gpt-oss-120b, reasoning_effort low, 600-token cap, 1 retry (gpt-4.1-mini if no Cerebras key) brain/llms.py: a 160-token cap truncated the greeting
TTFT p50 442 ms, p95 1 714 ms (43 calls, 30 days to 16 Oct 2026, India) as_built §3: "the tail is the vendor's queue"
OpenAI from India ~850 ms TTFT for every model tried; LiveKit Inference no faster meghdootam/main.py comment
Planned questions spoken word for word after a ≤ 6-word acknowledgement hot_path.py: a paraphrased question once asked something else
Every model named circuit breaker, timeout, low retries as_built §4

Deviation: the design puts no model call here (Chair selects a pre-generated move in ~10 ms); the build makes one. With the endpoint wait, it is the whole gap to the 800 ms target.

Measure it

  • Metric — llm_node_ttft p50 and p95 per turn, by provider and region.
  • See it — per-turn metrics on the assistant message; split network from queue by timing a tiny request from the same pod.
  • Bounded by — a deadline and a fixed line; circuit breakers so an outage fails fast instead of queueing.

Pitfalls

Choosing the model by benchmark tokens per second

  • Why it's tempting: throughput is what providers advertise.
  • Why it's wrong: the person waits for the first token; from a far region it's dominated by the round trip and the queue.
  • Think instead: measure TTFT p95 from where your agent runs.

Letting the model rephrase scripted content

  • Why it's tempting: one prompt that "keeps the meaning" sounds more natural.
  • Why it's wrong: the model sometimes asks a different question, and everything downstream (scoring, coverage) assumes the planned one.
  • Think instead: the model writes the short acknowledgement; the fixed text is appended word for word.

Connections

… → endpoint → think → speak → … — the second-largest line in the turn.

  • shrunk by preemptive generation; removed by speculative pre-generation.
  • a budget line in the latency budget.
  • wire share owned by time to first token (networking).
  • Say it: Q32

notes.title: Speculative Pre-generation — The Reply Is Ready When the Turn Ends
notes.html:
References

~/Projects/tech_documentation/utkarsh_architecture.md §2.1, §2.5 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_pipeline_capacity.md Part A · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/decision_rationale.md

TL;DR

While the person is still talking, a background tier prepares two to four fully written next moves from the partial transcript. When the turn ends, a rules-based picker selects one in about 10 ms. No model call sits between the last word and the first sound.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per turn

Flow: partial transcriptbackground drafts 2–4 movesturn endspicker selects ~10 msTTS

Recall

Prompt Answer
When are replies generated? during the person's speech, on partial transcripts
What happens at commit? selection over ready moves, not generation
What guards against a stale move? the move records which turn it was made for
What if no move fits? the next planned question, then a bridge line
The health metric speculative hit rate
Draw speech, background drafting and the commit on one timeline drafts overlap speech; commit → select → TTS with no model box

The idea

Without it: every turn pays a model's first-token time after the endpoint wait.

It does: moves generation into the time the person is speaking, which is free, and leaves only a cheap choice on the critical path.

It costs: model calls on drafts that are never used, a harder state model (moves keyed by turn, freshness checks), and a metric nobody has defined yet.

How it works

Fallback ladder (every turn has an answer) When
1. Best speculative move fresh for this turn, confidence above the floor
2. Next planned question no fresh move; always available, zero latency
3. Bridge line ("That's useful, let me build on that.") buys ~1.5 s while the tier finishes

Each move carries its kind (probe, advance, clarify, redirect, close), the TTS-ready text, what it's meant to evidence, a confidence, and generated_for_turn as a staleness guard.

Knobs

Knob Design value Raise it → Lower it →
Moves drafted per turn 2–4 better fit, more calls cheaper, more fallbacks
Confidence floor not set fewer odd moves, more planned questions more speculative moves used
Background deadline 1.8 s per drafting call richer drafts stale drafts cancelled sooner
Refresh on new words every final phrase fresher moves, more calls cheaper, more stale

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Speculative pre-generation the design's key mechanism; Chair selects in ~10 ms utkarsh_architecture.md §2.1
What's built instead rules pick the move, one model call phrases it, started early by preemptive generation as_built §2 row 8
Background tier today Assessor and Prober run on each final phrase and feed the picker FLOW §5
speculative_hit_rate no agreed definition decision_rationale weak point 4
Lever rank second, after the endpoint wait as_built §3 levers

Measure it

  • Metric — hit rate (turns answered by a speculative move ÷ all turns), wasted drafts per interview, and e2e_latency with and without it.
  • See it — log the ladder step chosen per turn (speculative, planned, bridge) and the draft's age.
  • Bounded by — the ladder: a planned question or a bridge line is always ready.

Pitfalls

Treating it as preemptive generation with a new name

  • Why it's tempting: both start the reply early.
  • Why it's wrong: preemptive waits for a final phrase and still calls the model after it; speculation keeps several finished replies in memory so commit is a lookup.
  • Think instead: preemptive shrinks the model line; speculation deletes it.

Shipping it without a hit-rate definition

  • Why it's tempting: latency improves on day one.
  • Why it's wrong: if most turns fall through to the planned question, the conversation stops adapting and nobody notices.
  • Think instead: define the hit rate first and alert when it drops.

Connections

… → endpoint → think → speak → … — takes "think" off the critical path.

  • replaces the model on the hot path.
  • needs a background tier that runs during speech.
  • is the full version of preemptive generation.
  • Say it: Q32 · Q41

notes.title: Latency-Tiered Agents — In the Turn, Beside It, After the Call
notes.html:
References

~/Projects/tech_documentation/utkarsh_architecture.md §2–3 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/FLOW_WALKTHROUGHS.md §5 · Voice agents (agentic pillar)

TL;DR

Split the agents by how long they may take, not by what they do: T0 must answer inside the turn, T1 works while the person speaks, T2 runs after the call. Only T0 is on the critical path; T1 is advice that may be late; T2 can be slow and thorough.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per turn

Flow: partial wordsT1 analysesinsight keyed by turnturn endsT0 picks the movespeakcall endsT2 scores

Recall

Prompt Answer
The three tiers and their windows T0 ≤ 800 ms in-turn · T1 2–20 s during speech · T2 30 s–5 min after the call
What does T0 do if T1 isn't ready? a cheap rule (short first answer → one probe)
Why keep the questioner and the scorer separate? a model is kinder to answers that fit its own question; and their budgets differ
Why does T2 run in a separate worker? its load comes after calls, and a lost report can't be recomputed from a lost call
Draw the three tiers against one interview's timeline T1 bars under the person's speech, T0 ticks at each turn end, T2 after the call

The idea

Without it: a supervisor fans out to five agents after each turn and reconciles them: 3–6 s of silence (ADD §2).

It does: lets only selection run in the turn, gives judgement the time the person spends talking, and leaves the score of record for after the call.

It costs: T1 can be late, so T0 must always have a fallback; and T0 and T1 share one event loop, where one blocking call is dead air.

How it works

Tier Window Runs (our names) Model class Where
T0 hot ≤ 800 ms, in the turn rules (intent_guard), the move picker (Chair), the voice (respond) small, fast, streamed agent process, main loop
T1 warm 2–20 s, during speech Assessor (provisional score), Prober (gap + hint), Sentinel (rules) mid same process, deadlined tasks
T2 cold 30 s–5 min, after the call Panel (independent scorers + reconciler), Reviewer, Scorer strong after the call

Rules that make it work: T1 writes insights keyed by turn outside the graph state (they would race on the checkpoint); T0 reads them if ready; T1 stands down on turns the guard marked as not-an-answer.

Knobs

Knob Our value Raise it → Lower it →
T1 debounce on new phrases 300 ms fewer restarts fresher insight
T1 call budget per interview 300 more analysis earlier fallback to the rule
T1 deadline per agent 0.9–1.8 s (design) richer insight late insights cancelled sooner

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
T0 + T1 one agent process per interview, shared state ADD §2, as_built rows 8–9
T1 → T0 InterviewContext.insights[turn]; fallback: first answer < 60 words gets one probe FLOW §5
Prober asks for a follow-up on 62% of complete answers FLOW §5, goldens/t1/ (open finding)
T2 runs in the agent process after the call today as_built row 12
T2 target a queue and a separate worker, so a killed session can't lose a report ADD §2.3, N7

Measure it

  • Metric — share of turns where T1's insight was ready at commit; T0's fallback rate; event-loop lag (alert at 50 ms, ADD §2.4).
  • See it — CHAIR … log reasons: prober: … vs no insight yet; short answer (41 words).
  • Bounded by — T0's rule fallback; T1's own call budget and deadlines.

Pitfalls

Putting the supervisor in the turn loop

  • Why it's tempting: it's the standard multi-agent pattern.
  • Why it's wrong: fan-out plus reconcile is seconds; the person hears silence.
  • Think instead: the supervisor selects from what the background already prepared.

Splitting tiers into services for "independent scaling"

  • Why it's tempting: separate scaling sounds like good architecture.
  • Why it's wrong: T0 and T1 are pinned to the same call and scale together; a network hop costs ~140 ms of the turn (ADD §2.2).
  • Think instead: split only where load or durability really differ, which is T2.

Connections

… → endpoint → think → … — what "think" is made of.

  • feeds speculative pre-generation — T1 is where moves would be drafted.
  • protected by guardrails beside the reply — T1 skips non-answers.
  • general pattern in conversational and interview agents.
  • Say it: Q39 · Q40 · Q41

notes.title: Writing for the Ear — Prompts Whose Output Is Spoken
notes.html:
References

LiveKit — Prompting guide (read 16 Oct 2026) · LiveKit — Modality-aware instructions · ~/Projects/convo_agentic/meghdootam/brain/hot_path.py (PERSONA, INSTRUCTIONS)

TL;DR

Everything the model writes will be read aloud, once, at speaking speed, with no way to scroll back. So: plain text, one or two short sentences, one question per turn, numbers and symbols written as they should be said, and any text that must be exact appended outside the model.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per turn

Flow: prompt: spoken rulesmodel writes 1–2 sentencesfixed text appended word for wordTTS

Recall

Prompt Answer
Formatting allowed in a spoken reply none: no markdown, lists, tables, code or emoji
Default length (LiveKit's guide) one to three sentences
How to handle numbers, emails, URLs spell them out; drop https://
Why one question per turn? a listener answers the last one and forgets the rest
Voice prompts should expect imperfect transcription, self-corrections, relative dates
Rewrite "Here are 3 options: 1) … 2) … 3) …" for the ear "There are three ways. The simplest is … Want the other two?"

The idea

Without it: a chat prompt reads asterisks and list numbers aloud, asks three questions at once, and spends 20 seconds on an answer the person stopped following after five.

It does: writes the rules of speech into the prompt, and keeps exact wording (questions, legal lines) out of the model's hands.

It costs: the model can't show structure, so long content has to be split across turns.

How it works

Rule Chat habit it replaces Why for the ear
One or two short sentences, then stop paragraphs each extra sentence is waiting time for the person
One question per turn "and also, could you…" people answer the last question only
No formatting markdown, lists, code TTS reads symbols or drops them
Spell out numbers, symbols, acronyms p95, k8s, $1.2k TTS guesses; the pronunciation lexicon fixes known terms (07 Speaking)
Expect ASR errors in the input taking text literally "item potency" may mean "idempotency"
Exact text appended, not paraphrased "keep the meaning" the model sometimes changes the question

Two views on fillers: LiveKit's guide suggests SSML <break> pauses, filler words and varied openers for realism in a cascade. Our design avoids filler sounds and buys responsiveness with latency, except one planned bridge line in the fallback ladder.

Knobs

Knob Default Raise it → Lower it →
Sentence limit in the prompt 1–3 (LiveKit) richer replies, longer waits terse; may feel curt
Output token cap per model room to speak cut-off sentences
Separate voice and text instructions one prompt LiveKit Instructions(audio=…, text=…) per modality –

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Persona rules "one or two short sentences, then stop · never more than one question · plain spoken English, no lists, markdown, emojis or code · stay neutral" hot_path.py PERSONA
Acknowledgement at most six neutral words, then the planned question appended word for word INSTRUCTIONS["ask"]
Fixed lines redirect, caution, wait: no model CANNED in hot_path.py

Measure it

  • Metric — words per agent turn, questions per turn (should be ≤ 1), share of replies with formatting characters.
  • See it — the agent transcript of a call, read aloud; anything you stumble on, TTS will too.
  • Bounded by — a token cap, and fixed text for anything that must be exact.

Pitfalls

Reusing the chat prompt

  • Why it's tempting: the same agent serves chat and voice.
  • Why it's wrong: chat rewards structure and completeness; speech punishes both.
  • Think instead: a voice variant of the instructions, or LiveKit's per-modality Instructions.

Asking the model to "keep the meaning" of scripted text

  • Why it's tempting: it sounds more natural than reading a script.
  • Why it's wrong: it sometimes asks a different question, and downstream scoring assumes the planned one.
  • Think instead: model for the connective words, fixed text for the content.

Connections

… → think → speak → … — shapes what the speak stage receives.

  • hands text to streaming TTS, via chunking and pronunciation.
  • keeps short, which helps time to first token.
  • carries the character defined in persona and personality.
  • general prompting in 05-AI-ML/08-Prompt-engineering/.
  • Say it: Q36

notes.title: Persona and Personality — Who the Agent Is, in Every Line
notes.html:
References

LiveKit — Prompting guide (read 16 Oct 2026) · LiveKit — TTS expressive mode · ~/Projects/convo_agentic/meghdootam/brain/hot_path.py (PERSONA, fixed lines) · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_pipeline_design.md §8.4

TL;DR

A voice agent's personality is heard in three places at once: what it says (the prompt and the fixed lines), how it says it (the voice, pace and emotion), and when (latency, interruptions). The design job is to make all three tell the same story, keep it the same from the first greeting to the last goodbye, and decide where warmth would cost fairness.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · design time

Flow: identity + roletone rulesmodel-written lines + fixed lines in the same voicevoice and pace that matchtested for drift

Recall

Prompt Answer
The three channels personality travels on words, voice (pace, emotion), timing
What breaks consistency most often? fixed lines and model lines written in different voices
LiveKit's guidance on emotion a calm baseline, stronger emotion only for specific moments; "appropriate emotion, not maximum emotion" (expressive mode)
Why must an interviewer stay neutral? praise or judgement in the call leaks the score and treats candidates differently
How do you test a persona? goldens that fail on praise, more than one question, repeated openers
Fill a grid: greeting, follow-up, redirect, caution, goodbye × warmth, firmness, words one row per moment; the same person in each cell

The idea

Without it: the model is cheerful, the fixed caution line is stern, the voice is flat, and the agent praises one candidate's answer and not another's. People hear three different agents.

It does: defines the character once (identity, role, tone, boundaries) and applies it to every line the agent speaks, generated or fixed, and to the voice that speaks it.

It costs: a persona with real warmth needs emotion control and more testing; a neutral one can sound cold if the timing is slow.

How it works

Layer Decide Our choice (Rachel)
Identity name, role, relationship to the person "Rachel, your AI interview prep buddy", running a mock screening
Stance warm, neutral, firm; what it never does warm at greeting and goodbye, neutral during answers: never praise or judge, never give answers or scores
Boundaries topics it refuses, how it refuses only questions about the interview; anything else: "keep to the interview", then carry on
Moments how the stance shifts redirect: brief, no blame · caution: firm, not hostile · ending for conduct: "calmly, without blame"
Voice timbre, pace, emotion range one voice for the whole session, slightly under natural rate, no synthesised "um"
Timing responsiveness buys warmth through low latency, not filler sounds

Fixed lines carry the persona too. Ours: "Let's keep our focus on the interview." · "Let's keep this respectful. I'm here to help you practise." · "Of course. Take thirty seconds, and start whenever you're ready." They are written in the same voice as the prompt, by hand, because no model writes them.

Emotion control (as of Oct 2026): LiveKit's expressive mode lets the model add emotion, pace and non-verbal tags that the TTS renders and the transcript drops; it needs LiveKit Inference with a supported provider (Fish Audio, Inworld, Cartesia, Gemini, SpaceXAI) and works in cascaded pipelines only.

Knobs

Knob Default Raise it → Lower it →
Warmth in the prompt product choice friendlier; risk of praise and bias in judged settings colder; feels like a form
Expressive mode (LiveKit) off emotion and pace vary by moment one even delivery
Disfluencies and non-verbal sounds on when expressive more human; read as manipulative once people know it's a system plainer
Pace provider default clearer for dense content when slightly slower faster turns

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Persona prompt Rachel, prep buddy, mock screening; one or two short sentences; neutral; refuses off-topic hot_path.py PERSONA
Neutral acknowledgement at most six neutral words before the planned question INSTRUCTIONS["ask"]
Persona test golden case passes only with no praise ("great!") and one question goldens/voice_interview_cases.md
Voice one voice per session, logged; Aura-2 Athena since 14 Oct 2026, chosen by ear design §8.4, as_built row 10
No filler sounds a synthesised "um" reads as manipulative; bridge lines are the honest way to buy time design §8.4

Measure it

  • Metric — praise or judgement rate in agent turns, questions per turn, opener repetition across a call, and listener ratings of "same person throughout".
  • See it — read one call's agent lines in order, generated and fixed together; anything that sounds like someone else is a persona bug.
  • Bounded by — fixed lines for the moments that matter most (caution, ending), and the persona golden cases in CI.

Pitfalls

Making an evaluator encouraging

  • Why it's tempting: warmth lowers anxiety and makes the product feel kind.
  • Why it's wrong: "great answer" to one candidate and silence to another signals the score and is unequal treatment.
  • Think instead: warmth at the edges (greeting, goodbye, asking for time), neutrality around answers.

Writing the persona only in the prompt

  • Why it's tempting: the system prompt is where "you are…" goes.
  • Why it's wrong: fixed lines, the voice and the timing also speak, and they ignore the prompt.
  • Think instead: one persona sheet that covers prompt, fixed lines, voice choice and pace, reviewed together.

Adding filler sounds to seem human

  • Why it's tempting: LiveKit's guide and expressive TTS make it easy.
  • Why it's wrong: in a judged conversation people know it's a system, and fake hesitation reads as manipulation.
  • Think instead: be human through timing and plain words; keep disfluencies for casual agents.

Connections

… → think → speak → … — decides the character before any line is written.

  • applies the format rules of writing for the ear.
  • sets the stance used by guarded moves (redirect, caution).
  • is voiced by choosing a voice.
  • Say it: Q43 · Q50

notes.title: Guardrails Beside the Reply — Draft and Hold
notes.html:
References

~/Projects/tech_documentation/FLOW_WALKTHROUGHS.md §4 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/as_built.md §2 row 8 · ~/Projects/convo_agentic/meghdootam/brain/gate.py

TL;DR

A guardrail model in front of every reply adds its latency to every turn. Instead, draft the reply and classify the turn at the same time, hold the draft for a short window, and release it if the label agrees, swap it if not, and send it anyway if the label is late.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per turn

Flow: final phraseguard starts earlyturn commitsdraft replyhold ≤ 0.9 sreleaseswaprelease

Recall

Prompt Answer
Why not run the guard first? it takes 340 ms to 2.6 s; that would be added to every turn
What runs before the model guard? regex rules; if they are sure, the model isn't asked
The hold window 0.9 s
A late label means treat the turn as an answer: fail open
Why does the guard label and never decide? the move stays with the picker, so limits and fallbacks apply in one place
Draw the three outcomes on one timeline label before draft (free), label inside the hold (≤ 0.9 s), label late (released)

The idea

Without it: either no model guard (rules catch 2 of 37 non-answers in our goldens) or a guard that adds up to seconds to every turn.

It does: speculative execution: the check costs nothing when it finishes before the first words are ready, and at most the hold window when it doesn't.

It costs: it fails open. A slow or broken guard lets an off-topic turn through as an answer.

How it works

Label Move Limit
off-topic, injection redirect: a fixed line, back to the question 2 per question
abusive caution, final caution, then wrap up 2 per interview
about the interview answer from a short list of facts 2 per question
asking for time fixed wait line per question

Redirect, caution and wait are fixed lines with no model: nothing a hostile turn can steer.

Knobs

Knob Our value Raise it → Lower it →
Hold window (HOLD_S) 0.9 s more labels in time, longer worst case fewer labels used
Guard calls per interview 240 – later turns on rules alone
Fail mode open fail closed: stalls or wrongly interrupts real answers –

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Guard Gatekeeper, qwen-3.8-27b on Cerebras, labels beside the draft FLOW §4, gate.py
Rules vs model rules 2 of 37 non-answers; model 36–37 of 37 intent goldens (FLOW §4)
Guard latency 340 ms to 2.6 s; the latency gate has both passed and failed with Cerebras load FLOW §4
Target guard on a different vendor from the speaker as_built row 8

Measure it

  • Metric — share of labels inside the hold, swap rate, late-label rate, guard p95.
  • See it — GATE off_topic [412ms] '…', GATE late (> 900ms): the reply goes out on the rules alone.
  • Bounded by — the hold window, the per-interview call budget, fixed lines for every guarded move.

Pitfalls

Letting the guard return the reply

  • Why it's tempting: one call that classifies and answers saves a step.
  • Why it's wrong: limits (2 redirects per question) and fallbacks live in the picker; a guard that decides bypasses them, and a steered guard steers the conversation.
  • Think instead: the guard returns a label; the picker returns the move.

Failing closed in a live call

  • Why it's tempting: safety first.
  • Why it's wrong: a slow guard then stalls or interrupts honest answers, which is the more common harm here.
  • Think instead: fail open on the label, keep the dangerous paths as fixed lines.

Connections

… → think → speak → … — safety without a serial step.

  • same pattern as preemptive generation — start early, discard if wrong.
  • tells the background tier which turns to skip.
  • general guardrails in 05-AI-ML/08-Prompt-engineering/10-Safety, Security & Adversarial Prompting/.
  • Say it: Q42

notes.title: Tools and Slow Work in a Turn — Never Leave Silence
notes.html:
References

LiveKit — Async tools (read 16 Oct 2026) · LiveKit — Prompting guide · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/FLOW_WALKTHROUGHS.md §6

TL;DR

A tool call that takes seconds is seconds of silence unless the agent speaks while it waits. Acknowledge at once, keep talking or stay politely quiet with a filler, deliver the result as a follow-up when it's ready, and let the person cancel or change the request mid-way.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per turn

Flow: requesttool startsagent: "checking that now"conversation continuesresult readyagent speaks it when idle

Recall

Prompt Answer
What blocks the conversation? a synchronous tool in the reply's path
LiveKit's mechanism (Oct 2026) async tools: status updates go into context and are voiced; the result is spoken when the agent is next idle
Filler audio ctx.with_filler() plays audio directly, bypassing the model, only in quiet pauses
Cancelling a running tool opt-in ToolFlag.CANCELLABLE, exposing cancel_task(call_id)
The person asks for time instead the same principle reversed: a fixed line, the question stays open
Draw a 6 s tool call with and without async handling without: 6 s silence; with: ack at once, talk, result spoken later

The idea

Without it: "let me book that" followed by six seconds of nothing; the person repeats themselves, which starts another turn.

It does: separates acknowledging, working and reporting into three moments, so the voice never goes dead.

It costs: results arrive out of turn, so the agent must voice them naturally later, and duplicate or stale requests need a policy.

How it works

Moment Agent says LiveKit (Oct 2026)
Request heard short acknowledgement the agent waits for the tool's first ctx.update(…)
Working progress, or filler in quiet pauses ctx.update, ctx.with_filler(delay, interval, max_steps)
Needs input asks, blocks other speech ctx.foreground()
Result a follow-up reply when idle the tool's return value
Changed mind cancel or replace CANCELLABLE; on_duplicate: allow (default), reject, replace, confirm

LiveKit's prompting guide adds: if an action fails, say so once, propose a fallback or ask; summarise structured results instead of reading identifiers.

Knobs

Knob Default (LiveKit, Oct 2026) Raise it → Lower it →
Filler delay 0 filler only on long waits filler at once
Filler interval none (plays once) repeats during long work –
on_duplicate allow replace or reject: no double bookings –

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Tools in the hot path none; slow work (scoring, probing) runs in the background tier ADD §2, FLOW §5
The person asks for time fixed WAIT_LINE, question stays open, not scored; narrow rule ≤ 10 words, else the guard decides FLOW §6
Bridge line a short acknowledgement that buys ~1.5 s, step 3 of the fallback ladder ADD §2.5

Measure it

  • Metric — longest silence per turn while a tool runs; share of tool results voiced after the person moved on.
  • See it — the gap between the acknowledgement and the result in the per-turn log.
  • Bounded by — tool timeouts and a spoken failure line.

Pitfalls

Awaiting the tool inside the reply

  • Why it's tempting: it's how a chat tool loop works.
  • Why it's wrong: the person hears silence for the whole call and starts talking over it.
  • Think instead: acknowledge, run it async, voice the result later.

Reading the raw result aloud

  • Why it's tempting: it's accurate and needs no extra prompt.
  • Why it's wrong: IDs, JSON and long lists are unlistenable.
  • Think instead: summarise in one sentence and offer detail.

Connections

… → think → speak → … — keeps "think" from blocking "speak".

  • uses the same rules as writing for the ear.
  • external tools and MCP servers in external tools and MCP.
  • sibling of silence and timeouts — silence from the other side.
  • general tool design in 05-AI-ML/03-Agentic-AI/03-Tool use-Function calling/.

notes.title: External Tools and MCP in a Voice Agent
notes.html:
References

LiveKit — Model Context Protocol, Tool loop design, Forwarding to the frontend (read 16 Oct 2026) · MCP (agentic pillar)

TL;DR

A voice agent can call the same tools as a chat agent, including whole MCP servers, but every call happens while a person waits in silence, every tool definition adds prompt tokens before the first word, and every action can rest on a misheard word. So: few tools, a timeout on each, speak before slow ones finish, read details back before anything that writes, and return sentences, not payloads.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per turn

Flow: turnmodel picks a toolslow? say a short lineMCP server or API, with a timeoutspeech-ready resultwrites: read back, wait for "yes"act

Recall

Prompt Answer
How LiveKit attaches an MCP server (Oct 2026) MCPToolset with an id, passed to tools (Python); mcp_servers is deprecated
The two MCP server types MCPServerHTTP (remote; /mcp streamable HTTP or /sse) and MCPServerStdio (local process)
The four tool rules specific descriptions, under 2 s, ToolError, meaningful (speech-ready) results
How many tools per agent (LiveKit) 5 to 10; beyond that, split across agents
What to return from a tool a speech-ready string with only what the agent needs to say
Guarding a write a read_back parameter the model may set only after reading details aloud; the code rejects it otherwise
Draw a turn with a 3 s tool call turn ends → tool starts → filler line at ~1 s → result → reply; writes add a read-back turn

The idea

Without it: a chat agent's 40 tools and raw JSON results go into a voice agent: the first word waits on a long prompt, a 3 s API call is 3 s of silence, and "book the 13th" is booked for the 30th.

It does: treats tools as part of the turn's latency and the turn's risk: a small, described tool set, timeouts, spoken progress, read-back before writes, and results phrased for the ear.

It costs: extra turns for confirmation, tools split across agents, and an MCP server's network hop and failure modes inside a live call.

How it works

The four tool rules (talk slide shared 16 Oct 2026, matching LiveKit's guidance):

Rule In practice Budget or API
Be specific in descriptions what it does, when to call it, when not to, valid values the model reads descriptions more closely than schemas
Keep tools fast target under 2 s; past ~1 s, speak first; past 2 s, make it async timeout on every external call
Handle errors with ToolError a reason the model can say or recover from bare exceptions → vague retries, apologies
Return meaningful data a speech-ready sentence with only what to say no IDs, no raw JSON

In detail:

Concern Rule (LiveKit guidance, Oct 2026) Why in voice
Tool count 5–10 per agent; split with handoffs or a supervisor each definition is prompt tokens before the first word
Descriptions what it does, when to call it, when not to; valid parameter values spelled out the model reads descriptions more closely than schemas
Slow tools if it can take more than ~1 s, speak first (session.say() filler, async tools) silence reads as a dropped call
Timeouts every tool that calls an external system has one a hung API is a hung conversation
Writes read details back; read_back flag enforced in code; disable interruptions during the write misheard numbers and names; a half-done write
Results speech-ready strings IDs and JSON are unlistenable
Errors raise ToolError with a reason the model can say bare exceptions cause vague retries and apologies
Chaining max_tool_steps (default 3) per turn caps a silent tool loop
Client-only data forward the call to the frontend over RPC (perform_rpc, 5–10 s timeouts in LiveKit's example) location, UI actions

MCP specifically: servers initialise in parallel at session start; one that fails is logged and the agent still starts. Filter with allowed_tools (by name) or filter_tools(); send auth as headers; set client_session_timeout_seconds. Agent-level tools replace session-level ones rather than merging. Python only as of Oct 2026 (livekit-agents[mcp]~=1.8). What MCP itself is, its transports, auth and security: the agentic pillar owns it.

Knobs

Knob Default Raise it → Lower it →
Tools visible to the model all attached more capability, slower first token, worse choice faster, more accurate selection
allowed_tools per MCP server all – only what this agent needs
max_tool_steps 3 longer chains, longer silences replies sooner with less
Tool timeout per tool fewer false failures faster fallback line
Read-back on writes off safer, one more turn faster, misheard actions

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
External tools or MCP on the hot path none: the interviewer only selects and phrases moves hot_path.py; slow work is in the background tier
Slow work scoring and probing run as background analysis during speech, not as tool calls latency tiers
Client-side action pause is an RPC from the client to the agent (the reverse direction) side channels
If tools were added read-only lookups first; writes behind read-back; MCP servers filtered per agent –

Measure it

  • Metric — tool latency p50/p95 per tool, silence while a tool runs, tool error rate, read-back refusals, prompt tokens added by tool definitions.
  • See it — per-turn llm_node_ttft with and without the toolset attached; tool spans in the trace.
  • Bounded by — timeouts, max_tool_steps, filler lines, and read-back on writes.

Pitfalls

Attaching a whole MCP server because it's one line

  • Why it's tempting: MCPToolset makes every tool available at once.
  • Why it's wrong: dozens of tool definitions slow the first token on every turn and make the model pick worse.
  • Think instead: allowed_tools down to what this agent needs; split the rest across agents.

Acting on what the STT heard

  • Why it's tempting: the transcript looks right on screen.
  • Why it's wrong: "thirteenth" vs "thirtieth", one digit of a phone number; the person never sees the transcript.
  • Think instead: read the details back and require a yes before any write.

Letting a slow tool run silently

  • Why it's tempting: the result will come.
  • Why it's wrong: after a second of silence people repeat themselves, which starts a new turn.
  • Think instead: say a short line at once, or make the tool async and voice the result later (tools and slow work).

Connections

… → endpoint → think → speak → … — tools inside a spoken turn.

  • extends tools and slow work (async tools, filler audio).
  • adds prompt tokens counted in the model on the hot path.
  • misheard input explained in vocabulary and streaming STT.
  • protocol owned by building vs consuming MCP servers and MCP at scale.
  • Say it: MCP Q11 (ten servers, four hundred tools) · MCP Q13 (when not to use MCP)
